newsitem.title: CHINA: Profits of China's Dajiang down, outlook gloomy.
newsitem.headline: Profits of China's Dajiang down, outlook gloomy.

text.p: Shanghai Dajiang (Group) Co Ltd, one of China's biggest feed grain producers, reported a 39.49 percent fall in 1996 net profits, and analysts said on Tuesday fierce competition would limit improvement.
The company has been a victim of its own success, the analysts said.
Strong growth in both feed grain and chicken meat sales in 1994 and 1995 had attracted a host of competitors into the market who have forced prices down, they said.
Dajiang scores high points for good management, but is still a "sell" for most brokers with a ruthless price war on feed grain continuing and the export market for chicken meat very weak.
"It's a well-managed company in a cyclical business," said Bruce Richardson of HG Asia in Shanghai.
"It has good prospects for the future, but I won't change my sell recommendation until I see the effects of the current price cutting on feed grains," he said.

The company's 1996 net profit was 118.72 million yuan, down from 196.19 million yuan in 1995 based on international accounting standards, a company statement published in Tuesday's Shanghai Securites News said.
"Dajiang's 1996 results are worse than we expected," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
"We believe local competition in the sale of animal feed will become even tougher because of the over-expansion of capacity over the past few years," she added.
In February this year, Dajiang cut the selling price of its animal feed by as much as 15 percent in an effort to secure its domestic market share.
But its main competitors, most notably the privately owned Hope Group, have at least matched every price cut, analysts said.
Exports of chicken meat, another major profit earner for Dajiang, are also not promising due to oversupply and competition, particularly in the huge Japanese market, they said.

"Around a third of its chicken meat is exported to Japan and prices fell nearly 50 percent in 1996 due to competition from South Korean chicken products," said another foreign brokerage analyst. "That dampened Dajiang's profit a lot."
Another problem, the analysts said, was sharp price increases in the past couple of years for Dajiang's main raw material, corn.
On the positive side, there are signs that some of the smaller feed grain producers are going out of business in the face of the cut-throat competition, and sales are rising again, analysts said.
"The company is pursuing an aggressive pricing strategy which has shown increases in sales volumes over the past two months," HG Asia's Richardson said.
"Management says they expect 10 percent growth in profits in 1997 and there may some upside even to that," he added.
Dajiang's B shares ended Tuesday's trade at $0.504, marginally up $0.004 or 0.8 percent from Monday's $0.500 on thin volume of 12,000 shares.
